study.title: Local constraints on alcohol--thioalcohol analogs in G35.2N

cover.headline: Radio telescope data show **alcohol and thioalcohol molecules appear in consistent ratios** across a star-forming cloud.

slides.title: Sulfur chemistry in star-forming regions is poorly understood because we can't identify where the sulfur hides.
slides.body:
Dense clouds where stars form contain complex organic molecules built from carbon, oxygen, and sulfur. For oxygen-bearing molecules like methanol we have detailed inventories. For their sulfur cousins, the thioalcohols, the chemistry remains murky.

Comparing structurally matched pairs like methanol and methanethiol offers a direct way to trace how sulfur behaves differently from oxygen in the same environment. That matters for understanding what feeds planet-forming chemistry.

slides.title: Three locations in the G35.2N cloud all showed methanol outnumbering methanethiol by a factor of 100 to 110.
slides.body:
Column density measurements from ALMA Band 6 observations gave methanol abundances between 1.8 and 2.7 × 10¹⁸ cm⁻², and methanethiol between 1.7 and 2.6 × 10¹⁶ cm⁻². The ratio stayed consistent across all three positions within measurement uncertainty.

The methanol-to-ethanol ratio also held steady at 31 to 32, matching values seen in other chemically rich sources. Ethanol-to-ethanethiol comparisons remain uncertain because many literature measurements provide only lower limits.

slides.title: The methyl-level alcohol-to-thioalcohol ratio is now the best empirical probe of sulfur organic chemistry in these environments.
slides.body:
Earlier surveys showed wide variation in the methanol-to-methanethiol ratio from source to source, suggesting local chemistry or ice history matters more than universal gas-phase pathways. These new constraints tighten the measurement in one location and add benchmark values for comparison.

The ethyl-level comparison would be more powerful but needs deeper observations of ethanethiol, which is harder to detect. Until then, the methyl pair remains the cleanest window into oxygen-versus-sulfur chemistry where planets eventually form.

caveats: Measurements come from three positions within one star-forming region, not a statistical sample of multiple sources.
Ethanethiol detection at one position remains tentative, limiting confidence in the ethyl-level alcohol-to-thioalcohol comparison.

caption: Radio telescope observations reveal that methanol and its sulfur analog methanethiol appear in stable ratios across different spots in a star-forming cloud, even as absolute abundances vary. The three measurement positions in G35.2N all showed methanol outnumbering methanethiol by roughly 100 to 1, offering a consistent benchmark for sulfur chemistry where planets eventually form. Published in Astronomy & Astrophysics using ALMA Band 6 data from three spectral-extraction positions in the MM3–MM5 region of G35.2N. Measurements rely on local thermodynamic equilibrium modeling and isotopologue proxies to handle optical depth. Full study: doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202661403 — Send this to anyone who insists sulfur chemistry is too messy to quantify in star-forming environments.
